body: Hello @allenwp , i think there's a way to keep compat, if you put a clamp checkbox that's on by default.

Good idea!

But this actually won't work either because the current behaviour is that clamping happens in Mobile/Forward+ and clamping does NOT happen in Compatibility. With this context, it makes it clear that it is a bug: the behaviour in Compatibility is correct and the behaviour in Mobile/Forward+ is incorrect.

This means that there is no way to have a clamping checkbox that maintains behaviour in all renderers.

Thinking and talking this through, it is now clear to me that this is probably best described as a `bug` and not a `breaks compat`. I'll re-work the GitHub labels to reflect this, but feel free to voice thoughts if you think my reasoning might be wrong.
I see that the clamping in gles3 was there but commented. Do we know why?

I don't know why, but I have a guess based on reviewing all of shader the files in Godot:

1. When the linear to sRGB function was first added to a shader, the places that used it either required clamping or did not support any HDR functionality, so the clamping made no difference. Because of this, clamping was added to the function for convenience so that you didn't need to call the function and follow up with clamping -- instead you could just call one function. This resulted in the original linear to sRGB function with clamping in `post.glsl` and `tonemap.glsl`. This was the root problem because the code was not clear that clamping was not a strictly a part of the linear to sRGB transformation, but instead was just a convenience. This is supported by the C++ linear to sRGB function that does not perform clamping.
2. This function with clamping was copy-pasted throughout the Godot codebase, without regard to whether it made sense to have clamping in each case.
3. When `post.glsl` was optimized to the approximation for linear to sRGB, the clamping was removed because it was extraneous shader instructions. At this point, it was probably easy to see that the clamping was not needed for the cases that called this copy of the linear to sRGB function so regard was made to whether the clamping was actually needed, unlike most other places in the codebase. The original non-approximation code was left as comments in this function (which is why you see the clamping is commented out).
4. The linear to sRGB functions were added to the visual shader nodes. In this process, they were simply copy-pasted from `post.glsl` for the approximation (Compatibility) and `tonemap.glsl` for the non-approximation (Mobile and Forward+). Again, like in point 2, no regard was taken to whether this clamping was actually needed for this case and the functions were blindly copied.
5. I separated clamping from the linear to sRGB functions in `tonemap.glsl` to better support HDR rendering and higher quality/consistent colour adjustments code, even with HDR values.

And so we have a bug where clamping is happening in some linear to sRGB functions where the code was blindly copied without consideration to whether it was actually needed. This is not only the case with the visual shader nodes, but also SMAA. SMAA will be fixed with the Windows HDR PR because this is where the bug is visually present. Other places that this PR touches might also not need the clamping, but I've moved them out of the function to solve the root problem (point 1) and also maintain existing clamping behaviour.
CC @clayjohn  git blame points at you making the change and commenting away the clamping https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blame/master/drivers/gles3/shaders/tonemap_inc.glsl

Clay does not have time to review such a minor bug fix. I've requested review from @blueskythlikesclouds; Whenever you have time, please take a look at the PR description text and see [this comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113956#issuecomment-3805215621) for an explanation as to why I believe this is simply a bug.

> This is a bit confusing to me. Does it even make any sense to use LinearToSRGB with values above 1.0? I thought SRGB only made sense in the 0.0-1.0 color range.

The sRGB transfer function can be used to encode colour data of an unbounded negative and positive range and the function can be inverted to decode back to the original colour data. Perceptual uniformity is somewhat achieved in the near-zero to `1.0` range, which makes it well suited for encoding colour data to an 8-bit buffer that is limited to the [0,1] range. Values above `1.0` will not achieve the same level of perceptual uniformity as values below `1.0`, but that doesn't mean that these values are not useful. Godot has used this concept of "overbright" colours and the colour picker allows you to pick overbright colours that will be stored in floating point formats with this nonlinear sRGB encoding. Additionally, I believe that the compatibility renderer with HDR 2D enabled also writes sRGB-encoded values to a floating point buffer during scene rendering to maintain overbright colours for use with HDR effects like glow.

> In the linked issue, the visual shader converts a potentially HDR framebuffer to SRGB, which again doesn't really make sense to me. Can converting HDR values to SRGB actually return meaningful values?

For some more context, here is the reason that some people want this behaviour: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/80868

One of the purposes of this node is to maintain sRGB transparency blending behaviour when using HDR 2D. If you are using HDR 2D, then you likely want to maintain HDR colour values, not clamp them. This is what the [linked issue ](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/113952)describes.

> If so, it should be safe to remove the clamping. I don't think this would break user shaders in a harmful way.

Note that there is no clamping in this shader node when using the Compatibility renderer. So if there are any issues with this behaviour, they would be seen with the existing Compatibility renderer.

Sorry, I resolved [Calinou's comment](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/113956#discussion_r2850092505) and pushed a little too quickly. I've made some more changes to the comments and also introduced a change to the compatibility documentation.

Basically, the comment about the approximation behaving poorly was partially correct. Here's a comparison of sRGB functions and the approximates that the Compatibility renderer uses:

linear to sRGB: https://www.desmos.com/calculator/d2clv3xu40
sRGB to linear: https://www.desmos.com/calculator/uzl8bover6

Although values above 1 behave reasonably, the approximations do not work with negative values. I've updated the comments in the glsl files to better describe this and also updated the user-facing documentation to make a note about how negative values are problematic.

My intent with this PR was to fix the mobile and forward+ behaviour, but the comments and documentation for Compatibility also needed updating.

(In summary: behaviour remains the same to the previously approved state of this PR; I only changed comments and documentation.)

> Although values above 1 behave reasonably, the approximations do not work with negative values. I've updated the comments in the glsl files to better describe this and also updated the user-facing documentation to make a note about how negative values are problematic.

In this case, should we not at least force the color to be 0.0 minimum? The Desmos graph for the compatibility method indeed looks messed up, so I doubt anyone actually relied on that.

Let's not complicate this PR though, so nevermind!

> Nitpicking but I noticed typos in your latest push.

Thanks! I appreciate these little nitpicks -- definitely no intention with a typo :)

> In this case, should we not at least force the color to be 0.0 minimum? The Desmos graph for the compatibility method indeed looks messed up, so I doubt anyone actually relied on that.
> 
> Let's not complicate this PR though, so nevermind!

Yes, changing how the sRGB approximation functions behave is outside of the scope of this PR. But, since Godot supports negative lights in the Compatibility renderer, I believe there is work to be done in a separate PR to make sure that this approximation is being used correctly and will never be given negative values.

In that separate PR, we can also revisit the shader graph node for Compatibility with one of these approaches:
1. Keep the status quo
2. Clip to non-negative before applying the approximations
3. Use the actual sRGB function instead of the approximations (it's possible the shader graph node doesn't need to use an approximation like the internal lighting calculations which go back and forth between linear and sRGB many times with additive lighting.)

I somewhat lean towards option 3 because if a user wants a faster approximation of sRGB in their own shader, they can simply copy-paste whatever approximation they'd like. In fact, they might want to use a 2.23(ish) power function to approximate instead of this one for those cases.

Anyway, yes, definitely better for a followup PR.
